name: StarRise at North Weld Village
headline: High Plains Housing Development Corp. built StarRise, a 58-unit permanent supportive housing building for chronically homeless adults at 30% AMI on a donated former produce-warehouse site at 123 9th Avenue in north Greeley, with a $1,450,000-a-year 2023 Round One 9% award from CHFA; residents began moving in on 2025-10-01 and it was full by 2025-12-23.
why_it_matters: It is a finished, fully leased example of a small nonprofit pairing 9% credits with a donated site, Division of Housing project-based vouchers on every unit, a Greeley-Weld Housing Authority property tax exemption partnership and roughly a quarter of the cost in local and philanthropic money, and it leased up in about 90 days through coordinated entry.

status.label: Open and fully leased: move-ins began 2025-10-01; full by 2025-12-23
status.detail: Groundbreaking was on 2024-06-20 and the contractor lists a May 2024 to September 2025 construction period. The Gazette reported residents began moving in on 2025-10-01 and the building was full on 2025-12-23; in June 2026 it won Housing Colorado's Project Eagle Award and People's Choice Award. The CHFA placed-in-service date is not public.

next_step: Watch for High Plains' CHFA tax credit application for Phase 2 (the Phoenix Project), which the executive director expects to file in February 2028.

key_numbers.meaning: Every unit is set aside for people experiencing chronic homelessness with a disability, with Division of Housing project-based vouchers so tenants pay 30% of income.
The full amount requested; about $14.5M over 10 years (inferred). No state credit is shown on CHFA's report.
About $466,000 per unit (inferred); construction itself was about $16.8M to $18.0M depending on the source.
Move-ins started 2025-10-01 and the building reached full occupancy 2025-12-23.

facts.value: 123 9th Avenue, Greeley, CO 80631 (Clayton neighborhood of north Greeley)
New construction, permanent supportive housing; 58 units, 58 low-income

6.5-acre infill former North Weld Produce Co. property (a 1908 cannery later used for onion storage), donated by Dennis Hoshiko in 2020; in a qualified census tract; rezoned from Industrial Light to Mixed Use High Intensity before the 2023 application

One four-story, wood-frame (Type V-A), sprinklered, two-elevator building attached to a renovated 1934 brick industrial building that holds the common space (food pantry, fitness area, maker space, kitchen, offices, health provider room)
About 56,024 sq ft per BizWest's project listing; about 60,000 sq ft per the MEP engineer
Trauma-informed design (assessment by Shopworks Architecture with 22 service providers and shelter residents in October 2022); NGBS Bronze target; heat pumps; all-electric ready and solar ready
The site was in the 100-year floodplain at application, so the first floor was raised; the city had asked FEMA to remap it to the 500-year floodplain
Housing First, filled through the Northern Colorado Continuum of Care coordinated entry system
One block from the Greeley-Evans Transit hub; near Sunrise Community Health clinics and Weld County Human Services

money.note: 2023 Round One award, equal to the request. The application named NEF as the equity investor (letter of interest).
Committed at application (about 10% of the cost); later described as a Weld Trust Flagship Award.

background.text: StarRise is Phase 1 of a planned five-phase North Weld Village campus. Phase 2, the Phoenix Project, is planned on the site of the original cannery building, which the Gazette reported was recently destroyed by fire; it is planned as 50 units for very low-income households, with a CHFA credit application expected in February 2028 and construction by May 2029. Earlier statements had described Phase 2 as 90 units.
High Plains was set up in 1994 by the City of Greeley, Weld County and United Way of Weld County, developed three tax credit properties (64 units) in its early years, and reorganized in 2018.
The application said local support made up about 25% of total development cost ($6.5 million), and that no CHFA basis boost or underwriting waiver was needed.
At a January 4, 2023 neighborhood open house (98 neighbors invited by mail in English and Spanish) no residential neighbors attended; the only business response was positive.

Supportive services are funded from operating cash flow, Medicaid billing, Division of Housing tenant support services money, a capitalized service reserve and paid developer fee, per the application.
KCI Construction says it helped High Plains prepare the LIHTC application in January 2023.

discrepancies.text: CHFA's reports print the sponsor as High Plain Housing Development Corp, while the sponsor and its partners use High Plains Housing Development Corp.
The architect lists a construction cost of $16,772,779, while the general contractor lists $18,032,647.
BizWest reported the groundbreaking on 2024-06-20 and the contractor gives a May 2024 start, while the Gazette says construction began in July 2024.
BizWest's project listing gives 56,024 sq ft, while the MEP engineer describes about 60,000 sq ft.
Phase 2 was described as 90 units in 2023, but as 50 units in the Gazette's 2026 article.
